lessons.title: Calculating Material Costs per Window or Door
lessons.body: To price any window or door, you first need to know exactly what it costs you in materials. Start by measuring the frame. For a standard 1.2m x 1.5m window, you need aluminum profiles: top, bottom, left, right, and a middle horizontal bar. Each profile length is cut from standard 6-meter bars. Calculate total linear meters: for this window, the perimeter is (1.2+1.5)*2 = 5.4m, plus the middle bar 1.2m = 6.6m. But you must add 10% for cutting waste, so buy 7.3m. Aluminum bars cost about $12 per meter in many African cities, so 7.3m x $12 = $87.60. Next, glass: for a 1.2x1.5 window, you need two panes of 0.6x0.7m (since the middle bar splits it). Glass costs $25 per square meter, so area = 0.6*0.7*2 = 0.84 sqm, cost = $21. Add rubber seals: 6.6m at $0.50/m = $3.30. Add screws, handles, and hinges: about $8. So total material cost = $87.60 + $21 + $3.30 + $8 = $119.90. For a door, say 0.9m x 2.1m, perimeter = 6m, plus a lock stile and maybe a mid-rail. Aluminum: 6m + 2m = 8m, with waste 8.8m, cost $105.60. Glass or panel: often 0.8m x 1.8m = 1.44 sqm, at $25 = $36. Hardware: lock, handle, hinges = $25. Total material = $105.60 + $36 + $25 = $166.60. Always use a notebook or phone app to record these costs for each job. Keep receipts. Update prices every month because aluminum and glass prices change. This gives you the true material cost before labour and profit.

lessons.title: Pricing Your Products for Profit
lessons.body: Once you know material cost, you must add labour, overhead, and profit. Labour: if you pay a worker $10 per day and he makes two windows per day, labour per window is $5. But you also work yourself. Include your time. For a standard window, set labour at 30% of material cost. For the $119.90 window, labour = $36. Overhead includes rent, electricity, transport, and tools depreciation. If your monthly overhead is $300 and you make 30 windows per month, overhead per window = $10. So total cost = material $119.90 + labour $36 + overhead $10 = $165.90. Now add profit. A common mistake is to add only 10%. In aluminum fabrication, aim for 30-50% profit margin on total cost. For 40% profit, selling price = cost / (1 - 0.40) = $165.90 / 0.6 = $276.50. That may seem high, but customers expect quality. Check competitors: if they sell similar windows at $250, you can price at $260 and still profit. For doors, material $166.60, labour 30% = $50, overhead $10, total cost = $226.60. At 40% profit, price = $226.60 / 0.6 = $377.70. Always quote a price that includes installation if you offer it. Installation adds transport and labour: add $20 per window. Never negotiate below your total cost. If a customer pushes, offer a smaller size or simpler design. Use a simple formula: Selling Price = (Material + Labour + Overhead) / (1 - Profit Margin). Keep a price list for common sizes. Review prices every three months.

lessons.title: Managing Cash Flow and Buying Materials
lessons.body: Cash flow is the money moving in and out of your business. Many aluminum workshops fail not because they lack profit, but because they run out of cash to buy materials. For example, you get a big order for 10 windows. You need $1,200 for materials upfront. If you have only $300, you cannot start. So you must manage cash carefully. First, always ask for a deposit. A 50% deposit on a $2,500 order gives you $1,250, enough to buy materials. Use that deposit only for that job's materials. Keep the rest for labour and overhead. Second, buy materials in bulk when prices are low. Aluminum prices often rise, so if you have extra cash, buy a few extra bars. But don't tie up all your cash in stock. Keep at least $500 as emergency cash for small repairs or transport. Third, track every job's cash: money in from customer, money out for materials, labour, transport. Use a notebook or a simple spreadsheet. At the end of each week, calculate how much cash you have. If you have less than $200, you cannot take new orders until you collect payments. Fourth, collect payments on time. For large jobs, split payments: 50% deposit, 40% on delivery, 10% after installation. If a customer delays, follow up politely but firmly. Fifth, separate business cash from personal cash. Open a separate bank account or mobile money wallet for the business. Pay yourself a fixed salary, say $100 per week, instead of dipping into job deposits. This discipline keeps your business alive.

lessons.title: Finding Reliable Suppliers in Your Area
lessons.body: Your business depends on reliable suppliers of aluminum profiles, glass, and hardware. Start by asking other fabricators in your area. They know who delivers on time and who sells fake profiles. Visit local hardware stores and aluminum distributors. In many African cities, you can find suppliers in industrial areas or large markets. For example, in Nairobi, go to Industrial Area; in Lagos, try Ladipo or Alaba markets. When you meet a supplier, ask three questions: 1) Do you have a price list? 2) How long does delivery take? 3) Can I return defective materials? Test them with a small order first. Buy one or two bars and check quality. Look for the grade of aluminum: 6063 T5 is common for windows and doors. Avoid thin profiles that bend easily. For glass, find a supplier who cuts to size accurately. Ask if they temper glass for doors. For hardware, buy from shops that specialize in aluminum accessories, not general hardware. Build relationships. Visit your supplier regularly, pay on time, and negotiate discounts for bulk orders. If a supplier is unreliable, find a backup. Always have at least two suppliers for each material. Keep a record of prices, phone numbers, and delivery times. Join a local fabricators' WhatsApp group to share supplier recommendations. When you find a good supplier, ask for a credit account after six months of prompt payments. That helps your cash flow.

lessons.title: Hiring and Training Apprentices
lessons.body: As your business grows, you cannot do everything alone. Hiring an apprentice is a low-cost way to increase production. In many African countries, apprentices learn on the job and receive a small stipend, not a full salary. Start by looking for young people aged 18-25 who are eager to learn. Ask family, friends, or local vocational schools for recommendations. When you hire, set clear expectations: working hours, tasks, and pay. For example, pay $3 per day for the first three months, then $5 per day after they can cut and assemble a simple window. Train them step by step. First, teach safety: always wear gloves and safety glasses when cutting aluminum. Second, teach measuring and cutting: how to use a tape measure, square, and hacksaw or cut-off saw. Third, teach assembly: how to fit corners, install glass, and attach handles. Use real jobs, not practice pieces. Show them once, then let them do it while you watch. Correct mistakes immediately. After one month, let them work on simple windows alone, but check their work. After three months, they should be able to make a standard window from start to finish. Pay them fairly and on time. Treat them with respect. A good apprentice can become your best worker. Consider sending them for a short course in welding or glass cutting if available. Keep a training log for each apprentice. After one year, you can hire them as a full employee or help them start their own workshop. This builds your reputation and creates a network of skilled workers.

lessons.title: Marketing Your Business Locally
lessons.body: Marketing does not require a big budget. Start with your immediate area. Tell everyone you meet: neighbors, shopkeepers, taxi drivers. Word of mouth is the strongest marketing in Africa. When you finish a job, ask the customer for a referral. Offer a small discount, say 5%, for every new customer they send. Put a signboard at your workshop with your phone number and what you do: 'Aluminum Windows & Doors â Made to Measure'. Use your phone to take photos of every finished job. Post them on WhatsApp status, Facebook Marketplace, and local buy-and-sell groups. Always include your phone number. Create a simple business card with your name, number, and services. Give it to hardware stores, building contractors, and real estate agents. Visit construction sites and talk to foremen. Offer to quote on their window and door needs. Partner with local builders: give them a 10% commission for any job they bring. Attend community events and church gatherings; wear a branded T-shirt. When you get a call, respond quickly. Go to the site, measure, and give a written quote within 24 hours. Follow up after two days. Good service leads to repeat business. Ask satisfied customers to post a review on Google Maps if they can. Keep a list of all customers and their phone numbers. Send them a message every six months to ask if they need repairs or new windows. This simple system can keep you busy all year.

quiz.q: What is the first step to calculate material cost for a window?
options: A) Measure the frame and calculate linear meters of aluminum
B) Buy all materials from the cheapest supplier
quiz.explanation: You must measure the frame to know how much aluminum profile is needed.

quiz.q: For a 1.2m x 1.5m window, what is the total linear meters of aluminum needed before waste?
quiz.explanation: Perimeter is (1.2+1.5)*2 = 5.4m, plus a middle bar of 1.2m gives 6.6m.

quiz.q: Why should you add 10% to your aluminum length when ordering?
quiz.explanation: Cutting profiles results in waste, so you need extra material.

quiz.q: If aluminum costs $12 per meter and you need 7.3m, what is the cost?
quiz.explanation: 7.3 multiplied by $12 equals $87.60.

quiz.q: What is the glass area for a 1.2x1.5m window with a middle bar splitting it into two equal panes?
quiz.explanation: Each pane is 0.6x0.7m, so two panes give 0.84 sqm.

quiz.q: What is the total material cost for the example window in Lesson 1?
quiz.explanation: Sum of aluminum, glass, seals, and hardware gives $119.90.

quiz.q: How do you calculate labour cost per window?
quiz.explanation: Lesson 2 recommends setting labour at 30% of material cost.

quiz.q: If monthly overhead is $300 and you make 30 windows, what is overhead per window?
quiz.explanation: $300 divided by 30 equals $10 per window.

quiz.q: What is the formula for selling price with a desired profit margin?
options: A) Selling Price = (Material + Labour + Overhead) / (1 - Profit Margin)
B) Selling Price = Material + Labour + Overhead + Profit
C) Selling Price = Cost * Profit Margin
quiz.explanation: This formula correctly accounts for profit as a percentage of selling price.

quiz.q: For a total cost of $165.90 and a 40% profit margin, what is the selling price?
Why should you never negotiate below total cost?
options: B) Customers will not respect you
D) You will run out of materials
quiz.explanation: Selling below cost means you lose money on each job.

quiz.q: What is a good deposit percentage to ask for on a large order?
quiz.explanation: A 50% deposit covers material costs and protects cash flow.

quiz.q: Why should you keep business cash separate from personal cash?
options: A) To avoid spending job deposits on personal expenses
quiz.explanation: Separating cash prevents you from using job deposits for personal needs.

quiz.q: What should you do if you have less than $200 cash?
options: A) Stop taking new orders until you collect payments
quiz.explanation: Without cash, you cannot buy materials for new jobs.

quiz.q: What is a recommended payment schedule for large jobs?
options: A) 50% deposit, 40% on delivery, 10% after installation
quiz.explanation: This schedule ensures cash for materials and final payment after satisfaction.

quiz.q: How can you find reliable suppliers?
options: A) Ask other fabricators and visit local markets
C) Buy from the cheapest without checking quality
D) Wait for suppliers to come to you
quiz.explanation: Other fabricators know who is reliable, and local markets have suppliers.

quiz.q: What aluminum grade is common for windows and doors?
quiz.explanation: 6063 T5 is a standard grade for architectural aluminum.

quiz.q: Why should you have at least two suppliers for each material?
options: A) To avoid delays if one is out of stock
quiz.explanation: Having backups ensures you can always get materials at good prices.

quiz.q: When can you ask for a credit account from a supplier?
options: A) After six months of prompt payments
quiz.explanation: Building trust over time may earn you credit terms.

quiz.q: What is a good way to test a new supplier?
options: A) Place a small order first
D) Send a friend to check
quiz.explanation: A small order lets you check quality and delivery without risk.

quiz.q: What should you teach an apprentice first?
quiz.explanation: Safety must come first to prevent injuries.

quiz.q: How much might you pay an apprentice in the first three months?
quiz.explanation: Lesson 5 suggests a small stipend of about $3 per day initially.

quiz.q: After how long should an apprentice be able to make a standard window alone?
quiz.explanation: With daily training, three months is realistic.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a training log for each apprentice?
options: A) To track their progress and skills
quiz.explanation: A log helps you see what they have learned and what they need to improve.

quiz.q: What is the best marketing tool for a small aluminum business?
quiz.explanation: Personal referrals are powerful and free.

quiz.q: What discount can you offer for a customer referral?
quiz.explanation: A small discount encourages referrals without cutting too much profit.

quiz.q: Where should you post photos of your finished jobs?
options: A) WhatsApp status and Facebook Marketplace
quiz.explanation: Social media and messaging apps reach local customers quickly.

quiz.q: What commission can you offer builders for bringing jobs?
quiz.explanation: A 10% commission incentivizes builders to recommend you.

quiz.q: How quickly should you respond to a customer inquiry?
quiz.explanation: Fast response shows professionalism and wins jobs.

quiz.q: What should you do after completing a job?
options: A) Ask for a referral and follow up later
quiz.explanation: Follow-up leads to repeat business and referrals.
